Nothing’s AI Earbuds Will Serve as an All-in-One Conversation Recorder

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, phone-maker Nothing Technology is breaking away from its typical retro-inspired designs with a latest pair of AI-powered earbuds, as reported earlier by Bloomberg.
  • The Ear Note earbuds are designed primarily to maximize the recording functionality.
  • According to recent reports, the earbuds can capture and transcribe phone calls, while the charging case has its own microphone to record in-person conversations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, phone-maker Nothing Technology is breaking away from its typical retro-inspired designs with a latest pair of AI-powered earbuds, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The company confirmed via an X post that its Ear Note wireless earbuds will be available starting Dec. 8.

The Ear Note earbuds are designed primarily to maximize the recording functionality. While other AI earbuds have already hit the market, the Ear Note is the first to record both phone calls and in-person conversations.

According to recent reports, the earbuds can capture and transcribe phone calls, while the charging case has its own microphone to record in-person conversations. To mitigate privacy concerns, the case only records with a physical button press — a tell that could reveal when audio is being captured around the Ear Note user.

Sources indicate that nothing shared that the Ear Note will work with multiple popular AI agents, but the full list of compatible software has not yet been released. The Ear Note works in tandem with an app that stores recordings from the earbuds and case, creating transcriptions and summaries similar to those created by the popular Otter AI app.

The Nothing brand has developed a cult following for combining lifestyle and fashion trends in its suite of smartphones, headphones, speakers and watches.

Industry observers note that the full product lineup is built with modern hardware, but mimics warm, nearly retrofuturist design sensibilities. The blocky Ear Note charging case continues this trend while taking the organization’s tech in a new direction.

In the lead-up to the Ear Note’s reveal, Nothing CEO Carl Pei described the earbuds in an X post as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.”.

In a Bloomberg interview, Pei indicated that Nothing isn’t trying to create AI agents or software, but that the manufacturer has a “really interesting opportunity to be the hardware layer to AI.”.

It has been revealed that it’s presently unclear how much the Ear Note earbuds and case will cost when they’re released next month. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the organization hasn’t settled on a price just yet. The most expensive earbuds currently available on the Nothing store cost $149.

Whether you’re covering your eyes, plugging your ears or slapping a timepiece on your wrist, there’s now an ever-present option to record the world around you. Multiple companies have created their own versions of smart glasses, earbuds and watches with augmented reality capabilities.

Now that AI is the flavor du jour, these existing features are being enhanced by fresh ways to scan and interact with the surrounding environment. That means a lot of visual and auditory data is being recorded by wearable devices, and very rarely with the consent of all parties involved.

The most immediate risk factors are associated with video recording – public distrust of smart glasses is so widespread that they’ve colloquially been coined “pervert glasses,” as folks fear they fundamentally break an unspoken social contract by obscuring public recording from other people.

But audio recording, enabled by Apple’s latest smartwatches, the Amazon Bee, Plaud earbuds and the upcoming Ear Note, is also raising concerns, not least because many states require all-party consent before you can record conversations.

The Ear Note’s ability to record every bit of audio, from phone calls to in-person conversations, means it will be handling more sensitive information than other AI-powered earbuds. The company will need to face latest challenges to ensure security measures are in place to prevent private chats from leaking.

It has been revealed that at the very least, it seems as though Nothing Technology is aware of these privacy risks. According to Bloomberg, the organization created a data and security team to address concerns that cropped up during the Ear Note’s development. The company has also “obtained the same privacy certifications as competing recording products and worked with law firms to assess potential risks and safeguards.”.

Pei called wearables with recording functionality a sensitive space, and remarked the design team was “extra careful to not take any risks.” The Ear Note earbuds and case are largely controlled by user commands, including tactile button presses that begin the recording process.

  • Grand Theft Auto 6 has dominated everyone's attention since it came out last week and broke the record for the most day one retail sales in entertainment history.
  • It has been revealed that according to X user @derrickgott007, they received a notice from PlayStation Safety saying their account was being temporarily suspended from using social features for 30 days after breaching the manufacturer's code of conduct regarding pornographic or obscene content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apparently just because it’s in the game doesn’t mean sharing “obscene” content is okay.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has dominated everyone's attention since it came out last week and broke the record for the most day one retail sales in entertainment history. Unfortunately, not everyone's experience has been 100 percent positive, especially now that one player has been hit with a social ban on PSN after sharing a photo of naked people taken with the game's built-in camera feature.

It has been revealed that according to X user @derrickgott007, they received a notice from PlayStation Safety saying their account was being temporarily suspended from using social features for 30 days after breaching the manufacturer's code of conduct regarding pornographic or obscene content. The concern is that the user claims the offending image was actually a photo taken using GTA 6's camera feature of a nudist resort they found inside the game before sharing it with someone else on PSN.

Industry observers note that in this case, if you simply go by what's outlined in PlayStation's code of conduct, technically this player did break the rules as there's a specific bullet point about not sharing, soliciting, accessing, distributing or storing "material that is obscene, pornographic, or illegal." However, where things get a bit murky is that the source of the offending material came from a game being played on a PS5 that is also sold digitally by Sony itself. This feels a bit hypocritical as it seems that it's okay for a game to contain nudity or pornographic material, but as soon as you take a photo or screenshot of said content, suddenly you're in violation of PlayStation's guidelines.

Furthermore, while a social ban might not sound that bad as the user will still have access to some games, because online multiplayer falls under the umbrella of social activity, @derrickgott007 states they can't even play Call of Duty during their 30-day suspension.

Another interesting topic that incidents like this bring up is how often regular people agree to things they haven't fully read or acknowledged due to a manufacturer's terms of service (ToS) or end-user license agreement (EULA). Often, these documents are so long and onerous that people blindly skip past them and hit the checkbox just so they can use the thing they paid for. Some organizations like the ToS;DR project have made efforts to call out companies with terms of services that are unnecessarily dense or difficult to understand, but it remains an ongoing issue for almost everyone in modern society.

Sadly, even though PlayStation's guidelines seem a bit contradictory, this incident should serve as a public service announcement to anyone considering taking a photo or screenshot of potentially obscene material in GTA 6 (or other games) with their PS5, as they need to be extra careful or else they risk getting hit with a similar ban.

We've also got further confirmation the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera.

Sources indicate that apple seems to have adopted a newly introduced strategy for the iPhone launch, splitting it into two phases. After launching the premium iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo in September, Apple is preparing new versions of the lower-priced models — and it looks like they'll look a lot more like the more expensive iPhones. CAD images of the new iPhone 18e seen by Engadget show a redesigned camera bump on the back of the phone, similar to the one on the Pro models. The images come from a source familiar with Apple's supply chain who who had previously shared accurate tips on the colors of the iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro before they were revealed.

In a recent development, the current iPhone 17e doesn't have a camera bump — instead, the lens has a small protrusion and sits flush against the back of the phone, with the microphone and LED flash also embedded in cutouts directly in the rear glass. But according to CAD images seen by Engadget, Apple appears to be considering changing that with the iPhone 18e. The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone. It's somewhat similar to the camera module on the M5 iPad Pro (which you can see in the image below).

Interestingly, it seems that the iPhone 18e will be the only model to feature this upcoming camera plateau. The same files include the CADs for the base iPhone 18 and the iPhone Air 2, both of which are expected to launch alongside the 18e next spring. The base iPhone 18 will keep the exact same design, but now with a thicker camera module — increasing from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches). Apple has been using the same 48-megapixel Sony IMX904 sensor for its base models since the iPhone 15, so a thicker camera module could mean new sensors or upgraded cameras.

As for the iPhone Air 2, the CADs seen by Engadget corroborate previous rumors that Apple's ultra-thin phone will feature a second rear camera — not a surprise given that its single lens was one of the main complaints about it. Although the Air 2 will remain 5.6mm thick, the camera module will increase in thickness from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches), with the two lenses aligned horizontally. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the leaker Digital Chat Station and analyst Jeff Pu have all said Apple is adding an ultra-wide lens to the second-generation Air, and the CAD images back those reports up.

Industry observers note that also, the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are expected to keep the same Dynamic Island as current models rather than the smaller cutout on the iPhone 18 Pro. Of course, these changes may end up being scrapped and never see the light of day, since Apple still has some time before they hit the stores next year.

Figma employee sues, alleging firm forced her to confront harassers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Figma engineer is suing the design software company and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.
  • Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S.
  • “Figma was my dream organization for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Figma engineer is suing the design software company and its co-founder and CEO, Dylan Field, over allegations that she faced sexual harassment and retaliation while managers and HR repeatedly told her to confront the very people she accused of misconduct.

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Newly introduced York, alleges that Figma’s culture of “direct feedback” led managers and HR to make engineer Serry Park address harassment herself rather than investigate her complaints. Park, who joined Figma in 2022, alleges the company’s response damaged her career, compensation, and mental health. The lawsuit also alleges that Park, who is Asian, faced racial and gender discrimination, including performance criticism based on stereotypes that Asian women are meek, timid, and conflict-averse.

“Figma was my dream organization for a long time,” Park told TechCrunch in an interview before the lawsuit was filed. “It was a place where I felt that I could level up in my career, working on a lot of really cool, interesting things at scale.”.

In a recent development, park is seeking damages, a jury trial, and a court order prohibiting Figma from requiring employees who report harassment to confront their alleged harassers. She also wants the manufacturer to adopt and enforce a process for investigating harassment complaints promptly and confidentially.

According to recent reports, when reached for comment, a spokesperson for Figma stated, “Figma does not tolerate discrimination or harassment. Figma also does not tolerate extortion. These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court.”.

Park told TechCrunch she initially had faith in Figma’s complaint process, expecting that if she documented the alleged harassment and reported it to the right people, the tech giant would act. But as an engineer in a male-dominated field, Park told TechCrunch, “I don’t feel that they took me seriously throughout this process.”.

Sources indicate that park, who is still employed at Figma, joined its San Francisco office in October 2022. Within weeks, her onboarding mentor — a fellow engineer — asked her on a date and continued pursuing her after she declined, Park alleges. She initially feared reporting him, worrying that her manager would “dismiss her reports or view her as the problem,” according to the lawsuit.

Park notes she tried to avoid her onboarding mentor. In early 2023, for example, she delayed choosing a work project until he had picked one. When her manager criticized her for not being a “team player,” Park explained that she was trying to avoid the colleague she accused of harassment, according to the suit.

Her manager allegedly dismissed her concerns, saying he had “met his wife at work too” and treating the behavior as “harmless flirtation.” When Park asked to be kept off projects with the onboarding mentor, HR allegedly instructed her to confront him directly about his behavior.

It has been revealed that the lawsuit ties that response to Figma’s culture of direct feedback, which Park alleges Field established and enforced. It says the company’s People organization trains managers to direct employees, including those reporting harassment, to give feedback directly to the person involved.

According to recent reports, in March 2023, her manager assigned him to a major project she was leading, despite her request to be separated from him. Park told her manager that she would “figure it out,” but alleges that having to work with him affected her performance. Her manager gave her a 2 out of 5 on her performance review, criticizing her for not speaking up enough or engaging with others and for lacking presence. Park was put on a coaching blueprint, which she completed in late 2023.

Industry observers note that changing managers didn’t help, according to the lawsuit. Her second manager also refused to separate them, allegedly telling Park that someone at her level should be able to resolve conflicts with teammates and that separating them would be “avoiding the problem.” Like her previous manager, he allegedly pointed out that he had met his partner at work.

Park alleges the harassment continued throughout 2023.

In April 2024, she transferred to another team, a move she claims set back her career by resetting her performance and promotion timeline.

Industry observers note that on her new team, which had more women, Park stated she felt better and no longer had to work with her alleged harasser. Her performance reviews improved, but in late 2025, she alleges another incident of sexual harassment, this time by her new manager.

It has been revealed that the incident followed a night out for drinks with her wife and two teammates, including her manager. The next day, during a team lunch, the manager allegedly remarked Park’s sex life had been discussed the previous evening. Park, who said no such conversation had occurred in her or her wife’s presence, felt “horrified and humiliated” by comments she believed fetishized queer relationships.

Recent findings suggest that A colleague reported the comments to HR as sexual harassment, according to the suit. Weeks later, Park’s manager apologized in a Slack message, saying she didn’t recall what she had noted. When Park sought HR’s guidance, she was again told to address the matter directly with her manager.

During their conversation, the manager allegedly became defensive, and the encounter left Park feeling “crushed, anxious, and vulnerable.” The manager also allegedly noted she would never make such a comment because she had “a lot of gay friends.”.

Recent findings suggest that the manager told HR that they had agreed it was a misunderstanding. HR closed its investigation without interviewing witnesses, according to the suit, even though Park disputed her manager’s account.

“Requiring an employee to confront her harasser as the price of complaining — and then closing her complaint — would dissuade a reasonable employee from complaining at all,” the suit said.

Park alleges her manager retaliated by publicly berating her, sometimes so aggressively that colleagues intervened or checked on her afterward, according to the lawsuit. The suit also alleges that other teammates left the team over concerns about the manager’s behavior.

Park again complained to HR about “escalating retaliation” and expressed concern the manager would “derail her career.” HR allegedly defended the manager’s conduct, saying the manager was “within her reasonable authority” and again instructed Park to address her concerns directly with the manager.

In early 2026, Park received another low performance review and a reduced bonus. The lawsuit alleges that similarly similarly situated men continued to receive promotions, raises, and bonuses. When Park reported the negative performance review to HR in March, she was allegedly told her sexual harassment complaint against her manager could not be “substantiated.”.

In a recent development, park took medical leave in March to receive treatment for PTSD symptoms and generalized anxiety. Cleared to return to work in June, she was prescribed workplace accommodations, including a graduated work schedule and mandatory remote workdays.

According to recent reports, park told TechCrunch that Figma approved the accommodations but had not implemented them at the time of the interview. In July, Park and her lawyers notified Figma of their intent to pursue legal action.

“It’s really scary for me,” she remarked about taking legal action. “I don’t know what’s going to happen next with this, I don’t know what the outcome is going to be, but at least it feels like this is my chance to do the right thing.”.

Your older, discontinued AirTags can still serve a purpose

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you toss your original AirTag, here are a few ways to keep it useful.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Earlier this year, Apple introduced the first fresh generation AirTag since the original debuted in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you toss your original AirTag, here are a few ways to keep it useful.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Earlier this year, Apple introduced the first fresh generation AirTag since the original debuted in 2021. And while you might still be able to find first-generation Apple AirTags for purchase on some websites, Apple doesn't sell them anymore. The company is now focusing solely on the new model and leaving the original AirTag behind. But the old ones are still supported in the Find My app, so there's lots of ways you can continue to use them.

Industry observers note that the newer Apple AirTag offers an expanded finding range thanks to the second-generation ultrawideband chip, upgraded Bluetooth chip, improved Precision Finding from up to 50 percent farther away and a louder speaker. Given how cheap Apple AirTags are ($29 on Amazon) and all the upgrades with the second-gen model, you'll probably want to grab a few for your most precious items.

Industry observers note that but that doesn't mean you should toss your old AirTags. They can be relocated to secondary items, kept as backups for your most vital gear or handed down to friends and family.

Sources indicate that an AirTag that still works is worth hanging onto. Use newer AirTags for your keys, purse, wallet, child's backpack and maybe even pet collar and move your old AirTags to secondary items. Toss one in your glove compartment or trunk of your car in case of theft or to keep track of your newly licensed teen if they turn off location sharing in Find My. Or put one in your luggage as a secondary method of tracking its location if it's lost or misplaced.

Keep one in your child's jacket pocket so they're still trackable if they don't have their backpack (some parents even stitch them into their kids' shoes). Clip one secondary set of keys you often misplace in the house, like the key to the back door or home office filing cabinet. While the range is farther and the speaker louder on the newly introduced AirTag, both are still sufficient on the older model for finding items within the home. My son used Precision Finding with an old AirTag the other day to locate his house keys and it worked perfectly well.

Industry observers note that you could also get creative and affix one to the inside of your headphones case or toss one in your dressy purse, clutch or wallet so you don't have to move the latest AirTag back and forth when you switch. Or keep one with items that are tough to find in a cluttered space, like holiday decorations in the attic, a toolbox in the garage or a small remote in the game room. AirTags use easily replaceable CR2032 batteries that last about a year with normal usage and under normal conditions.

In a recent development, since the upcoming Precision Finding benefits of the second-generation Apple AirTag are only supported with iPhone 15 and newer models, you won't be able to use one if you have an older phone. In this case, it's still worthwhile to continue using a first-gen Apple AirTag until you upgrade your phone. Standard Precision Finding works with iPhone 11 through 14 models, so consider handing over the old AirTag to a friend or family member with an older iPhone, like a parent or grandparent. They can use it for their wallet, purse, eyeglasses case or other item they often misplace.

If you want to be extra diligent, use a second older AirTag with a upcoming battery as a backup in case the battery in your new AirTag dies before you get the chance to replace it. A second AirTag can also add security. Think putting the new AirTag under your bicycle seat and the older one under the bike's bottle cage or inside the bell. A thief might find one and dispose of it, but likely won't find both.

Some buyback sites in certain countries also purchase old AirTags. While Apple doesn't accept AirTags for trade-in, sites like Sell Techs in the UK and BuyBackWorld do. So you could make a bit of cash by selling them. Just because older AirTags are slowly becoming obsolete, that doesn't mean they don't still have their use.

Latest Update: An unseen planet past Neptune may be in Earths weight class

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Math points to our solar system having another planet in Earth's weight class far beyond Neptune, tugging distant icy bodies onto strange orbits, a latest study proposes.
  • It has been revealed that that would make it far smaller than Planet Nine, a hypothesized giant world five to 10 times Earth's mass that has drawn most of the attention in the hunt for an undiscovered planet.
  • "Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our solar system, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time," said lead researcher Patryk Sofia Lykawka, of Kindai University in Japan, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Math points to our solar system having another planet in Earth's weight class far beyond Neptune, tugging distant icy bodies onto strange orbits, a latest study proposes.

It has been revealed that that would make it far smaller than Planet Nine, a hypothesized giant world five to 10 times Earth's mass that has drawn most of the attention in the hunt for an undiscovered planet. No one has spotted this suspected world, nicknamed Planet X2, but these researchers argue it would explain the strangest orbits in the outer solar system better.

"Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our solar system, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time," said lead researcher Patryk Sofia Lykawka, of Kindai University in Japan, in a statement.

Every search for a missing planet has started the same way, with something in space that doesn't add up. In the 1800s, astronomers noticed Uranus wasn't staying on its predicted path, and the culprit turned out to be Neptune. Percival Lowell thought Uranus was still misbehaving and went looking for a "Planet X," a search that led to Pluto in 1930. But Pluto proved far too small to explain the trouble. Today, clues come from farther out, in a growing collection of frozen worlds beyond Neptune that move in ways the known planets can't explain. To many astronomers, that hints that something is still out there — maybe one planet, maybe more.

Beyond Neptune, a vast spill of icy leftovers from the solar system's birth circles the sun. Most of these objects travel in the Kuiper Belt, a broad band 38 to 50 times as far from the sun as Earth. Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found more and more of these objects on steeply tilted or stretched-out orbits.

It has been revealed that in the new study, the researchers built a computer model of the young solar system. It included the four giant planets, thousands of small icy bodies, and 1,500 Pluto-size worlds. Then, the computer worked out how each body tugged on the others, step by step, across 4.5 billion years. When the team added Planet X2, up to twice Earth's mass, its gravity pulled some icy objects out of Neptune's reach and tipped others onto steep angles. Together, those effects reproduced the orbits of every known oddball, including Sedna, a distant world that swings far beyond the planets on a long, narrow loop. Models without the planet fell far short, according to the paper, published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Every hidden-planet study relies on computer models, but this one seems to replay more of the solar system's history. Early on, Neptune slowly drifted outward from the sun. As it moved, its gravity flung some icy objects far out and trapped others in orbits that march in step with Neptune.

Lykawka's own 2023 model skipped that drift and didn't include the main Kuiper Belt, where most known icy objects travel. It demonstrated that Planet X2 could create the odd distant orbits, but not whether the planet would also wreck the parts of the belt that Neptune built. In the newly introduced model, Planet X2 creates the strange distant orbits and leaves the rest of the belt much like what astronomers see today.

Industry observers note that A competing idea — that a few extra Mars- to Earth-size worlds formed among the giant planets and got flung around early on — fared worse in the team's model. The giant planets would have thrown those worlds out of the solar system within tens of millions of years — too fast to explain the strange orbits seen today.

According to recent reports, planet Nine faces problems of its own. Its backers proposed it after noticing that the orbits of a few distant icy objects seemed to point in roughly the same direction, as if something big had herded them into line. Other researchers have argued that the pattern may be a fluke, caused by having too few known objects and by telescopes watching only certain patches of sky. Several recently discovered distant objects follow orbits that don't fit what Planet Nine predicts, the authors say.

It has been revealed that in the researchers' best-fitting models, Planet X2 circles the sun at an average distance of about 33 billion to 46 billion miles. That's roughly 12 to 17 times as far out as Neptune, and nine to 13 times as far as Pluto. Even at its closest, the planet would stay nearly 19 billion miles from the sun — more than six times Neptune's distance. Its orbit would likely tilt only slightly from the path the other planets follow.

"If this planet exists, it could change how we understand the history of our solar system and how its most distant objects came to follow such unusual orbits," Lykawka stated.

Sources indicate that the researchers admit the model doesn't fix everything. For example, compared with what a major sky survey found, the simulations predicted too few objects in the larger orbits the team studied.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which photographs the night sky again and again, could settle the debate, catching the planet as a faint, slowly moving dot. That's a tall order for something so far from the sun's light. Another possibility is that Rubin could find enough distant icy objects to show whether their orbits carry Planet X2's gravitational fingerprints.

"We now have an opportunity to put this idea to the test," stated study co-author Jonti Horner, a professor at the University of Southern Queensland, in a statement. "As the Rubin Observatory surveys the sky, we will find latest clues that help us understand the distant reaches of the Solar System — and whether another planet is still waiting to be discovered.".

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

According to recent reports, the latest Halide enhancement also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

In a recent development, lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo revision let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

In a recent development, today’s upcoming XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The patch revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III debuted back in May with a redesigned camera and the upcoming Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available.
  • Canva today confirmed “AI Controls,” a new toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.
  • Generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

Canva today confirmed “AI Controls,” a new toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

Generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:.

For some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

To give its users the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

Put simply, this is great to see.

AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

Sources indicate that while wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

Upcoming in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the upcoming slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

It has been revealed that there’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Recent findings suggest that for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other key parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Sources indicate that unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It has been revealed that it’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

According to recent reports, proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Industry observers note that proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new users and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

In a recent development, connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

According to recent reports, the NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the newly introduced word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Sources indicate that players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

Bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report indicates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tomorrow marks the Full Moon, but tonight's Moon already looks almost full.
  • Sources indicate that as of Monday, Nov.
  • According to recent reports, if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Tranquillitatis and Fecunditatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tomorrow marks the Full Moon, but tonight's Moon already looks almost full. It's still technically in its Waxing Gibbous phase, with just a small portion of its surface left in the darkness.

Sources indicate that as of Monday, Nov. 23, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 97% of its surface visible.

According to recent reports, if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Tranquillitatis and Fecunditatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau. With binoculars, you'll also see the Grimaldi Basin, the Endymion Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 15, and 16 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

Sources indicate that according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a Upcoming Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

It has been revealed that first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#2879. What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (657 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • Industry observers note that this arrangement also reveals how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

Industry observers note that this arrangement also reveals how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this newly introduced material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the tech giant when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Sources indicate that things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila declared looks for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, states Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a substantial one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

In a recent development, the glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

Recent findings suggest that china dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.).

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

It has been revealed that “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our organization. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”.

#2878. How to use AI glasses as a teleprompter

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

How to use AI glasses as a teleprompter

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you have the right type of smart glasses, this is an easy feature to enable.
  • According to recent reports, out of all the myriad variations of smart glasses available today, the ones with built-in waveguides — such as the XGIMI MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 — have the most utility.
  • These glasses also have a built-in teleprompter mode that lets you deliver presentations or speeches while maintaining eye contact, and honestly, they're pretty good at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you have the right type of smart glasses, this is an easy feature to enable.

According to recent reports, out of all the myriad variations of smart glasses available today, the ones with built-in waveguides — such as the XGIMI MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 — have the most utility. Having a screen projected in your field of view that indicates notifications, turn-by-turn directions or real-time translations is particularly useful outdoors. The best part about using the MemoMind One and Even G2 is that these smart glasses don't have a camera, so there's no social stigma to using them outside.

These glasses also have a built-in teleprompter mode that lets you deliver presentations or speeches while maintaining eye contact, and honestly, they're pretty good at it. As the waveguides project the screen in your field-of-view, it feels natural to use glasses as a teleprompter. I tested the MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 with this mode, and here's what you need to know.

The MemoMind One and Even G2 have a teleprompter feature that's easy to use; just load the script into the app, and you can select how fast (or slow) to scroll the text. Even's G2 reads PDF, plaintext, and DOCX files, but MemoMind One has just TXT and DOCX, with no PDF integration. This is mildly annoying if you regularly deal with PDF documents, but at least converting documents between file formats is trivial these days.

That noted, MemoMind One has greater control over how you can view and control the teleprompter text. You can easily adjust font size, line width (which is a nice bonus), and adjust the display scaling just for the teleprompter. Both smart glasses have a nifty auto-follow feature that slows down or speeds up the text based on your speaking cadence. The feature (ostensibly) relies on AI to listen to your speech and adjusts the flow of the text accordingly. Other than that, you can get an auto-scroll option set to words per minute, and there's manual control as well.

Using the MemoMind One and Even G2 as a teleprompter is easy. I loaded up my Find X10 Pro Max review script and started talking, and the MicroLED-based waveguides did a good job projecting the text without otherwise inhibiting my field-of-view. You get to see the time elapsed (which is useful for me), along with battery level of the glasses and the current time. I don't routinely use a teleprompter, but having smart glasses to do so is far less of a hassle than setting up a dedicated one (at least in my use case).

Sources indicate that the waveguide prisms aren't that noticeable externally (unless someone is standing within 15cm of you), so if you're in a public setting, the text won't be visible to anyone in your vicinity. If anything, smart glasses are a good option in a public speaking setting as it gives you greater mobility — your teleprompter moves with you. Also, both the MemoMind One and Even G2 have monochrome waveguides with good brightness levels, and I didn't see any problems making out the text while outdoors. I found the MemoMind One to get brighter than the G2 in outdoor use.

Recent findings suggest that I've been using the Even G2 and MemoMind One interchangeably for most of the last six months. The G2 is a decent upgrade to the G1, and I like that the case has an integrated charger — that's one less cable for me to store. MemoMind doesn't do that, so I need to store the tiny dongle carefully so I don't lose the only way to charge the glasses.

According to recent reports, both glasses are lightweight at under 50g, and while the Even G2 is lighter, I found the MemoMind One to be more comfortable to wear. Battery life is better on the MemoMind One, and the glasses have onboard audio and sound tuned by Harman; they're great to listen to podcasts on the go. The G2 misses out on speakers altogether, so you don't get any built-in sound.

Recent findings suggest that where the MemoMind One truly wins out is the control mechanism. The Even G2 uses a series of taps and swipe actions to control the glasses, with the gesture surface located at the temple tips, which is just awkward to use. There's also the small fact that it doesn't register gestures correctly at times, so I'm often scrolling or trying to trigger a gesture by reaching behind my ear, and it isn't the best look if you're in public.

Thankfully, the MemoMind One doesn't have these shortcomings; the glasses have a physical button located below the right hinge, and it's easy to interact. A single tap lets you cycle between menus, and a long-press action is used to exit to the dashboard. The UI wasn't quite as polished at launch, but MemoMind rolled out a slare of software updates over the last three months, and the glasses are on par with the Even G2 in this area.

It has been revealed that out of these smart glasses, I'd get the MemoMind One if I had to pick one. The MemoMind One just feels easier to wear, you can select three frame styles (G2 is limited to two), and it costs $499, $100 less than the G2. That's if you're getting the standard model; if you use prescription lenses, you'll need to pay an additional $280 for the MemoMind One and $159 for the Even G2. Of the two, the MemoMind One has the better feature-set as it has built-in audio and brighter waveguides, and I found it easier to wear and use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

Sources indicate that there are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An crucial note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better.
  • While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year.
  • So what are you giving up that matters?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a upcoming device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list.

While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable.

So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 people, and new features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only big sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven.

Realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some substantial sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much?

Recent findings suggest that what makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro back display is a masterpiece - and Google needs to add it to android

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a big year for Xiaomi as the latest Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are launching globally.
  • Except, the Xiaomi 18 Pro has a serious secret weapon: the innovative back display.
  • It has been revealed that it's not the first Xiaomi Pro phone with a rear display, but it is the first to come globally, and it was worth the wait.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a big year for Xiaomi as the latest Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are launching globally. I've been using them for a week, and normally I’d promptly settle on it being “an excellent flagship smartphone that's super capable, but doesn't excite me as much as a folding phone.".

Except, the Xiaomi 18 Pro has a serious secret weapon: the innovative back display.

It has been revealed that it's not the first Xiaomi Pro phone with a rear display, but it is the first to come globally, and it was worth the wait. I'm absolutely blown away by the rear display, which is a masterpiece - it's so good, Google should make it part of Android.

Here's what it can do, why it's so good, and the feature that shows the future of Android smartphones.

Xiaomi isn't the first to experiment with second screens. Android has long had attempts to add extra screens, side edges for notifications, or Glyph displays/notification lights to tell you something.

Sources indicate that yet all of these felt like gimmicks. The closest we've come to a genuinely usable second screen is the Moto Razr, and that's because it's a folding phone and the cover display is just a small phone screen. None of them were inherently useful and even if they were at first, they quickly lost their utility.

Sources indicate that it turns out that there's a good reason for that. The onus is generally on the tech giant to provide an infinite number of options and use cases, and then predict what else you might like.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Then there's the added problem of persuading developers to upgrade their apps to use this real estate or, more likely, to create upcoming apps for it. Since the second iPhone, it's been clear that apps and experiences matter a lot for feature adoption, and a secondary display is no exception.

It has been revealed that it turns out there's a great answer to all of these problems: AI. That's the magic that makes this second screen inherently useful – giving you something you'll actually use multiple times a day.

Have you heard of vibe coding? It’s a term used to describe building apps and software with vibes, aka describing changes and having AI make them, rather than coding the changes yourself. I’ve been using it all year to build several platforms and apps, and it’s revolutionary. You can type simple English, and AI will make the changes.

In a recent development, google and Xiaomi have taken this concept further with a new feature called GenAI apps. As the name suggests, it stands for Generative AI apps, or using AI to generate entire apps with one message. This is the secret to making the secondary display more useful: instead of relying on a organization to build everything you need, you can build it yourself.

We’ve all been there: you’re stuck in the doctor’s waiting room, lying in bed, in a car, or otherwise just looking for something to do. Sure, you can play yet another game, or you can have some fun and create latest things to try on the back display. It takes three to five minutes to build a polished, optimized app specifically for the back display. Simply put: GenAI apps are magnificent, and a glimpse of how we’ll use our phones in the future.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro makes regular phones as exciting as a folding phone.

Recent findings suggest that think about how useful this is: playing DnD and you’ve lost the dice? Create newly introduced dice in just a minute on your phone. Want to pin your shopping list for when you go shopping? Easy. Love flipping coins? There’s an app for that. I created one in 3 minutes; it’s that easy – and the GenAI app's chat window had it as one of the suggested apps.

It’s not just about creating your own apps: Xiaomi has built a series of useful, fun, or interactive apps that are easy to use, from an activity and workout tracker to a ninja swipe game, and many more in between. The only real downside? You can install a maximum of 12 at a time, but it is super easy to install or remove them in just a few seconds.

Since Xiaomi first built the rear display, I’ve been waiting for them to give this a wow factor that makes it a necessity. GenAI apps offer that wow factor, since you can build whatever you want in just a few minutes. Yes, there are monthly limits on how many apps you can create, but nonetheless, I can’t stop using the Xiaomi 18 Pro back display.

In a recent development, as you might expect, there’s one further added benefit: it’s the perfect viewfinder for selfies. The back display solves the selfie problem: front cameras are usually lower quality than rear cameras, and rear cameras usually don't let you see what you are capturing (unless you're using a foldable).

Industry observers note that the Xiaomi 18 Pro rear display lets you use the full camera UX, including capturing in portrait or landscape based on the phone's orientation when you’re capturing. It’s essentially the same as using the main display, and surprisingly useful for selfies, especially as you can use gestures like holding your palm up to capture the photo.

Beyond that, Xiaomi added built-in support for Google Maps, Spotify, and YouTube Music on the rear screen – letting you glance at turn-by-turn directions or control playback without waking the main display – alongside widgets, panels, and a range of wallpaper and clock styles. One of my favorites lets you display different inspirational quotes, and considering how positive affirmations can be for your mental health, it’s a great face to have. There’s also a customizable Always On Display for glancing at pinned notes, widgets, or the time while your phone sits face-down.

In a recent development, I’m so enamored with the Xiaomi 18 Pro and its rear screen that there’s only one thing I want: for Google to make this the default in Android. Every Android phone maker should adopt this; Google should add full support in the core OS, and the Play Store should include a classifier for back-display apps.

This would solve the other key problem: you can build apps, but you can’t share them with anyone else. A future marketplace or way to surface apps other people have built would build momentum and also let people sell, earn, and do more. Considering how themes are often sold for a low price and theme stores are incredibly popular, I can see how this would be a win for all consumers.

In the meantime, I’m off to build some more Gen AI apps. The only thing limiting me? Deciding what to build next.

What is the best way to secure your PlayStation 5 for a flight?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that GTA 6 releases in November 2026, but unfortunately, you can't pause real life.
  • Recent findings suggest that the short answer is yes.
  • It has been revealed that this decision is ultimately up to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that GTA 6 releases in November 2026, but unfortunately, you can't pause real life. That business trip you had planned doesn't care about your other life in Vice City, so you'll have to get creative to keep playing while you're away from home. You might be asking yourself if you should just take your PlayStation 5 along with you, and frankly, nobody here is going to judge you for that. But is it even possible to carry a major, bulky gaming console with you on a plane?

Recent findings suggest that the short answer is yes. The TSA allows a PS5 in both carry-on and checked bags, but it recommends carry-on for fragile electronics. The only real problem with taking Sony's console along with you is the DualSense controller, which uses a lithium ion battery and needs some special care. The console itself just needs good padding. And if dragging your system through security sounds like too much for you, there is always the option of streaming remotely.

It has been revealed that this decision is ultimately up to you. Both the carry-on and checked-bag options present their own advantages and disadvantages. A carry-on means you'll have to, well, carry your PS5 with you the entire trip. That doesn't leave a lot of room for much else in your bag, but it also means you can keep an eye on your console at all times. Putting it in a checked bag frees up space for the flight, but with your system out of sight, you run the risk of an airport worker mishandling your luggage or losing it.

Industry observers note that no matter your choice, packing your PS5 carefully matters. In a carry-on, make sure you wrap your console with a sweater or some other padding, and pack the cables with it. If possible, it's best to keep the carry-on under the seat in front of you to avoid all the shoving and shifting in the overhead compartments.

In a recent development, in a checked bag, the ideal way to pack your PS5 would be in the original box or inside a hard shell, but that isn't always realistic. As an alternative, place the console in the center of your luggage and completely surround it with soft clothes. If you have a hard plastic suitcase, that would be preferable to a soft-sided bag.

According to recent reports, the DualSense controller has a lithium ion battery rated at 3.65 volts and 1,560 milliamp hours, which works out to about 5.7 watt hours. That is far below the 100 watt hour limit the FAA sets for lithium-ion batteries, so the controller is allowed on a plane. Still, the FAA says devices with lithium batteries should be carried in the cabin. If the controller has to be checked, it must be completely powered off and protected from damage or accidental activation. The reason is thermal runaway — a battery overheating and catching fire — which ULSE counted at an average of 2.36 incidents per week on passenger flights in 2025. In the cabin, flight crews are trained to recognize and respond to lithium battery fires.

So keep your controller with you, make sure it is turned off or completely out of juice, and wrap it in some clothes or place it in a protective shell to keep it from getting damaged. Your best option would be an official DualSense carry case, like the one that comes with the DualSense Edge.

Recent findings suggest that there is a third option that allows you to keep playing from anywhere without having to carry your PS5 with you, and that is PlayStation's Remote play. This alternative allows you to stream your games online using your phone, a tablet or a laptop via your home console. Sony requires a connection of at least 5Mbps and recommends 15Mbps for a smoother picture.

For this to work, you need to keep your home console running in rest mode with "Stay Connected to the Internet" and "Enable Turning on PS5 from Network" activated. You can find these options under Settings > System > Power Saving > Features Available in Rest Mode.

The PlayStation Portal makes this easier. It's a dedicated handheld that streams the PS5 over Wi-Fi. Sony states it works on public networks too, as long as it was first set up on the home network. Players with a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription can also use it to stream select games from Sony's servers with no console running at home.

Check the airline's carry-on size and weight limits against the console's dimensions.

Back up your save data and finish any pending updates.

Shut the console down completely, unplug everything, and take out the disc.

Wrap the power cable and HDMI cable, and pack them together with the console.

Pad the console in its original box, a hard case, or soft clothes toward the center of your luggage.

Switch the controller off and keep it in the cabin with you in a padded pouch.

At the hotel, make sure the TV has a free HDMI port before settling in.

#2872. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1048 w)
